characters: Jonathan: a 14-year-old SRC prefect in a school uniform, with a notebook and a pen.
Rahinatu: his classmate, 14, with a camera phone and a worried look.
Madam Mills: a waakye seller in her fifties, in an apron and headscarf, ladling food from a large pot.
Mr Zormelo: a municipal environmental officer, in a reflective vest, with a clipboard.

narrationPlan.voice: Lively street voices; a warm, dignified voice for Madam Mills; a clear voice for Jonathan
narrationPlan.pace: Lively and busy at the road, careful and persuasive at the letter (about 120 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Busy street sounds, sizzling and chatter; a clear, determined tune at the letter (placeholder)
culturalNotes: The school, sellers, officer and Municipal Assembly are invented. Food sellers are shown with respect: they feed their communities and earn a living. The story treats the problem as one that needs a plan made with the sellers.

The two effects (choked gutters and blocked pavements) and one solution (a designated food court) are examples. A different community may have different effects; teachers should help learners find evidence in their own area.
The letter on pages 6 and 7 is a model formal letter with the eight features. “Dear Sir” is used because the Municipal Chief Executive’s name is not given.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check the formal-letter format on pages 6 and 7 against the BECE marking scheme: the eight features, the two effects and one solution, and the link words.
Check that the story is fair to sellers and does not suggest that they alone cause the problems; some residents also dump waste.
Check the malaria and flooding statements with a health or environmental officer, and the food-court solution with a local planning officer.

teacherGuide.overview: A story that matches a typical BECE/WASSCE letter task: two adverse effects of food sellers on a community and one solution. It models a formal letter that follows every feature and treats the sellers fairly.
learningGoals: Write a formal letter with all eight features.
Organise two effects and one solution in separate, linked paragraphs.
Use polite, persuasive language with no contractions.
beforeReading: Ask: who benefits from the food sellers on your road? What problems can they cause?
whileReading: At pages 6 and 7, ask learners to tick the eight features in the letter.
afterReading: Write a formal letter to the Municipal Chief Executive about a problem in your own community, with two effects and one solution.
Interview a food seller about what they need.
discussion: How can a solution help both sellers and neighbours?
reflection: What is one thing you could do this week to keep your road clean and safe?

support: Give learners a paragraph frame: First… As a result… Second… Consequently… To solve this I suggest…
stretch: Write a reply from the Municipal Chief Executive, using formal language.

culturalNotes: The school, sellers, officer and Municipal Assembly are invented. Food sellers are shown with respect: they feed their communities and earn a living. The story treats the problem as one that needs a plan made with the sellers.

The two effects (choked gutters and blocked pavements) and one solution (a designated food court) are examples. A different community may have different effects; teachers should help learners find evidence in their own area.
The letter on pages 6 and 7 is a model formal letter with the eight features. “Dear Sir” is used because the Municipal Chief Executive’s name is not given.
localiseThis: Use real local places and your own Assembly’s title. Talk to real sellers, with their permission.

factCheck.claim: A formal letter has the writer’s address, the date, the recipient’s designation and full address, “Dear Sir/Madam”, a title or heading, “Yours faithfully/Yours sincerely”, the writer’s signature and full name; the language must be polite, clear and persuasive with no contractions or slang.
factCheck.explanation: From the formal-letter and essay criteria supplied by the project owner, including the two-part task of two adverse effects and one solution.
factCheck.reference: Project-owner marking guidance (organisation, expression, mechanical accuracy); verify against the official marking scheme.
